newsitem.title: USA: Ill. park districts welcome court ruling on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Ill. park districts welcome court ruling on taxes.

text.p: Illinois park district officials said Tuesday they were pleased that a DuPage County Circuit Court judge reversed his ruling in a controversial property tax tax case that stood to impact numerous district bond issues.
"I think (the ruling) puts at rest some questions that were outstanding about park districts' bonding ability," said Peter Murphy, general counsel of the Illinois Association of Park Districts.

The association had recently joined the lawsuit, brought by business taxpayers in the county, on the side of the DuPage County tax collector. The lawsuit focused on Lisle Park District as a test case, but any ruling in the case would have impacted several other park districts in the county.

Judge John Darrah ruled Tuesday morning that the application of an Illinois property tax limitation law to certain park district debt would violate the contract clauses of the Illinois and U.S. Constitution.

That ruling reversed Darrah's April 1996 decision that property taxes used by the Lisle Park District to pay off general obligation debt issued for the retirement of about $6 million of installment contracts and alternate bonds were subject to limitations under a 1991 state tax cap law.
The April ruling rendered void all taxes levied in excess of the limit and entitled the plaintiffs to a tax refund.

Steve Jeffress, superintendent of the Lisle Park District, said Darrah's previous ruling would have had a "dramatic" effect on the way the district did business. He said that ruling would have forced the district to seek voter approval of higher taxes to support bond issues.
The district had estimated it would have to refund $384,000 for taxes it levied to pay debt service from 1991 to 1994.

Despite the fact the attorney for the business taxpayers has said Darrah's new ruling would be appealed to the Illinois Appellate Court, Jeffress said his park district would continue to operate on the premise that its bond issuance was legal.
Murphy said that Darrah's previous ruling had prevented some districts from issuing debt. He added that the association was confident Darrah's new ruling would be upheld by the higher court.

Richard Makarski, an attorney at Chapman and Cutler, which served as special assistant DuPage County state's attorney in the case, said Darrah's new ruling could impact similar taxpayer lawsuits pending against about 20 park districts in Kane County.

The 1991 tax cap law subjected park districts and other local governments in five suburban Chicago counties to an annual limit in property tax collection increases of five percent or the rate of inflation, whichever was less. Any increases in taxes over that amount required voter approval.

Attorneys representing the park districts had argued that a 1983 amendment to the Illinois park district code allowed districts to issue GO debt to pay off installment contracts or to refund loans and that existing obligations to issue GO debt would be immune from any subsequent change in state law.
